candidates.attacker_control: The 'token' query parameter of the protocol-independent registration endpoint /realms/{realm}/login-actions/registration (GET and POST), and, secondarily, of the OIDC /protocol/openid-connect/registrations URL. The value is a self-crafted JWS whose payload the attacker fully controls (typ=ORGIVT, exp in the future, eml=attacker's registration email, org_id=target organization). Because parseInvitationToken() never verifies the signature, the attacker's signature is irrelevant.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that central action-token processing verifies the signature (LoginActionsService.handleActionToken lines 582-617 uses a SignatureVerifierContext plus realm-URL/active/nonce checks) and that the OIDC registrations entry point aborts for invalid tokens (AuthorizationEndpoint.register lines 240-250). However, the two protocol-independent registration entry points discard the returned error (LoginActionsService lines 765-767, 789-791) and RegistrationUserCreation re-parses the raw request token itself; TokenVerifier.getToken() (lines 421-426) and parse() (399-419) never call verifySignature()/verify() (433-468, 470-485). RegistrationUserCreation does check isExpired(), the typ claim and e-mail equality, but never the signature, issuer, audience or action nonce. addManagedMember performs no domain/broker verification (JpaOrganizationProvider lines 172-213). Verified the 'token' query parameter reaches the flow via AuthenticationProcessor.getActionUrl (lines 605-627) and that ErrorPage.error has no flow-terminating side effect (services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/ErrorPage.java lines 30-32). No runtime execution or diff against upstream was possible, so it remains possible that a runtime filter elsewhere rejects the forged token (not found in source).
candidates.impact: Unauthorized organization membership/authorization bypass: a self-registered attacker can join an organization they were never invited to (membership type MANAGED), gaining organization group membership that is used for organization-scoped roles/applications and organization membership claims, and potentially access through organization-associated identity providers; the same unverified token also controls the post-registration redirect URI (reduri).
candidates.prerequisites: ORGANIZATION feature enabled (declared Type.DEFAULT in common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/Profile.java, line 124) with at least one organization configured in the realm; attacker can reach the registration flow (realm self-registration allowed, or an organization context present) so a valid session_code/tab_id/execution can be obtained; attacker knows or can guess the target organization id; the registration e-mail matches the attacker-chosen token e-mail (attacker controls both).
candidates.root_cause: Organizations.parseInvitationToken() builds a TokenVerifier but only calls getToken(), which parses the JWS payload without invoking verify()/verifySignature() and without realm-URL, active or nonce checks. RegistrationUserCreation.validate() then trusts attacker-chosen claims from that unverified token (typ='ORGIVT', exp, eml, org_id) and stores it in the session; in the success phase addOrganizationMember() calls OrganizationProvider.addManagedMember() with the unverified org_id, joining the newly created user to that organization. The action-token verification that exists centrally (LoginActionsService.handleActionToken, line 601-617) is ineffective for this path because the protocol-independent registration GET/POST (LoginActionsService.registerPage/processRegister) ignore the error Response returned by preHandleActionToken (lines 765-767 and 789-791).
candidates.title: Organization invitation token accepted without signature verification during registration, allowing forged tokens to add a user to an arbitrary organization
candidates.trace: 1) Attacker starts registration (e.g. GET /realms/{realm}/protocol/openid-connect/registrations?response_type=code&client_id=account) and receives a registration form with session_code/tab_id/execution. 2) Attacker submits the registration POST to /realms/{realm}/login-actions/registration?...&token=<forged JWS>. 3) LoginActionsService.processRegister (lines 779-794) calls preHandleActionToken(tokenString), whose verification failure returns an error Response that is discarded; execution continues into registerRequest/processRegistration. 4) AuthenticationProcessor action URL handling shows the 'token' query param is propagated into the flow (AuthenticationProcessor lines 605-627). 5) RegistrationUserCreation.validate (lines 89, 290-335) calls Organizations.parseInvitationToken, which returns the token via TokenVerifier.create(...).getToken() without verify(); the only checks are orgId lookup, isExpired(), typ==ORGIVT and submitted-email equality - all attacker-satisfiable. 6) On success, RegistrationUserCreation.success -> addOrganizationMember (lines 337-350) calls provider.addManagedMember(orgModel, user). 7) JpaOrganizationProvider.addMember(user.joinGroup(group, MANAGED), lines 181-213) adds the membership without requiring a broker/domain relationship. Result: an uninvited user becomes a managed member of the target organization.
candidates.unverified: No runtime confirmation; exploitability depends on the realm having self-registration enabled (or an organization context) and on the attacker knowing the target organization ID. I could not compare against the upstream version of Organizations.parseInvitationToken, so I cannot determine whether the missing verify() call is an intentionally introduced regression or a pre-existing upstream bug - in both cases the source-level missing signature verification is present. The registration POST flow was traced statically only.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-347 Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature (authorization bypass)

coverage_summary: Source scope: 5,862 visible files (4,824 Java, ~360 JS/TS) under the assigned root; binary/NUL files are refused/skipped by the tools. The snapshot omits Java test sources, FreeMarker (*.ftl), *.tsx and *.adoc files, so template-rendering and Java-test-based evidence could not be inspected. P1 relation index: 5,808 files indexed, 54 source files missing from the index, syntactic-only relations (name/type/arity call candidates), no data flow, no control flow, no semantic resolution, no SAST verdict; 86,962 unresolved calls, so absence of an indexed edge is not evidence of absence. I inspected the highest-risk production paths reachable by remote users: OIDC auth/token/logout/userinfo endpoints, RedirectUtils, TokenVerifier/AuthenticationManager, PKCE, SAML service/broker signature paths, token exchange v1/v2, IdP account linking (IdpLinkAction/IdentityBrokerService), organization invite/registration flow, FGAP v1/v2 admin permissions, vault and theme resource loading, TLS trust managers. This is not an exhaustive per-file review of all 5,862 files; unexamined areas include large parts of model/JPA/Hibernate mapping, infinispan, operator, adapters, docs/config and most JS/TS UI code.
limitations: No code execution, build, test or scanner run: all conclusions are static source reasoning; nothing was runtime-confirmed.
The P1 index is syntactic/navigation-only (no data flow, no reachability, no semantic resolution); index labels and edges were not treated as vulnerability evidence.
Java tests and FreeMarker/TSX/Adoc files are absent from the snapshot, so test-based counterevidence and template-side sinks could not be reviewed.

I could not diff the snapshot against upstream Keycloak, so I cannot tell whether the missing signature verification is an injected regression or a pre-existing upstream defect; both would still constitute the reported vulnerability.
Exploitability depends on configuration prerequisites (registration enabled or organization context, target organization id known) that I could not verify at runtime.
Coverage of 5,862 files was prioritized, not exhaustive; other unresolved leads (noted in rejected_leads) may warrant follow-up.

rejected_leads.reason: RedirectUtils includes the wildcard/unsafe-path('%2f','..') protections and post-logout redirect validation uses verifyRedirectUri with required redirect; the commented-out HTTPS scheme check in PairwiseSubMapperUtils.resolveValidSectorIdentifier appears long-standing and its practical impact (sector identifier host only) is lower and not clearly exploitable from source alone.
S256/plain comparison and code_verifier format/length checks are present and match the expected behavior; no bypass identified in source.

The implementation verifies all Signature elements, rejects unsigned assertions mixed with signed ones, and uses raw encoded query parameters for redirect-binding signatures; no weakness found in the static trace.
Audience/holder/public-client checks, consent checks and refresh/offline restrictions are present; no source-evidenced bypass identified.
Feature-gated (ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2) and the reviewed evaluator delegations perform the expected canView/canManage/canImpersonate checks; no concrete bypass identified within review time.

rejected_leads.lead: FilesPlainTextVaultProvider path-traversal guard and legacy-key path (validate bypassed in AbstractVaultProvider.checkForLegacyKey)
rejected_leads.reason: Vault keys are administrator-controlled configuration, and the primary validate() performs a parent-path equality check; only a weaker hardening gap, not a strong attacker-controlled issue.

rejected_leads.lead: No-op X509TrustManager implementations (connections/httpclient/HttpClientBuilder.PassthroughTrustManager, JSSETruststoreConfigurator ANY policy, adapters cloned HttpClientBuilder)
rejected_leads.reason: They are explicitly opt-in via configuration (disable-trust-manager / HostnameVerificationPolicy.ANY) rather than default behavior.

summary: Reviewed the Keycloak (~26.3.0-SNAPSHOT) snapshot focusing on authentication, authorization, token verification, redirect handling, SAML, PKCE, admin permission and organization-invitation flows. The strongest source-evidenced issue is in the Organizations invitation flow: the invite token that authorizes joining an organization is parsed without any signature verification (TokenVerifier.getToken() only parses), and the unverified claims (org_id, eml, typ, exp) directly drive a managed-organization-membership grant during self-registration. The protocol-independent registration GET/POST entry points even compute but discard the action-token verification error, so a forged token is not rejected before RegistrationUserCreation consumes it. No runtime testing was performed; the finding is a source-evidence lead, not runtime-confirmed.
